newsitem.title: Vietnam: Hanoi fetes Japan's Hashimoto as aid pledges flow.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi fetes Japan's Hashimoto as aid pledges flow.

text.p: Vietnam rolled out the red carpet on Saturday as Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto began the fourth stage of a swing through Southeast Asia which has been overshadowed by the hostage crisis in Peru.

A military band struck up and a line of smiling girls in traditional Vietnamese dress waved bunches of flowers as Hashimoto arrived at the Presidential Palace in Hanoi, where he was greeted by Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet.

The latest leg of the Japanese leader's five-nation trip began after Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's government renewed talks late on Friday with Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
The talks aim to negotiate a peaceful solution to the 24-day-old crisis.
After inspecting the guard of honour with Kiet, Hashimoto signed a stack of new aid pledges worth some $765 million.

Japan is by far and away the leading donor of official development aid (ODA) to poverty-hit Vietnam, pledging $3.23 billion between 1992 and 1996. Of the record $2.4 billion committed by donors for this year, its share is about one third.
Its latest pledges include a loan of $736.4 million for nine projects aimed at improving the poverty-hit country's transport and electricity infrastructure and rural development.
Japan's ambassador to Hanoi, Katsunari Suzuki, said Hashimoto would reaffirm Tokyo's support for the communist country's decade-old drive to reform its economy along market lines.

"Japan will continue to support Vietnam's ongoing renovation policy..." he told the official Vietnam News Agency. "The two leaders will also examine measures to promote the relationship between Japan and ASEAN in the 21st century."

The Communist Party's official daily, Nhan Dan, said in an editorial that the two countries were determined to broaden a relationship which has in recent years hinged on aid, trade and foreign investment.
Now, with Vietnam a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Japan keen to boost ties with the seven-nation grouping, ties are likely to be closer.
Many older Vietnamese remember Japan's World War Two occupation of their country, which has been blamed for a devastating famine from 1943 to 1945.
But that era is rarely mentioned by politicians from either country these days.

Hanoi enjoys a trade surplus of some $750 million a year with Japan, while Japanese firms have earmarked $2.7 billion for investment projects in Vietnam -- placing their nation second in a long list of countries seeking a share in the booming economy.
After talks with Kiet, Hashimoto paid a courtesy visit to Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi.
On Sunday he is due to visit the mausoleum of Ho Chi Minh, the revered founding father of modern-day Vietnam, and a Japanese school before leaving for his tour's last stop, Singapore.
The Japanese leader -- who marked his first anniversary in office on Saturday -- is expected to give a key address on Tokyo's Asia-Pacific policy in Singapore on Tuesday.
